name: SI units and prefixes
teach:
When a problem mixes prefixes such as mm, km or ns, or gives a quantity in non-SI units such as km/h or cm$^2$, replace each prefix by its power of ten. Put the whole prefixed unit in brackets before squaring or cubing it. Then multiply the numbers.
$$\begin{aligned}&\mathrm{n}=10^{-9},\ \mu=10^{-6},\ \mathrm{m}=10^{-3},\ \mathrm{c}=10^{-2}\\&\mathrm{k}=10^{3},\ \mathrm{M}=10^{6},\ \mathrm{G}=10^{9}\end{aligned}$$

The core intuition here is that a prefix is only a power of ten. Converting the unit name but not the number, or forgetting that a squared unit squares the factor, gives answers wrong by powers of ten.

*Example:* Convert an area and a speed to SI.
$$6.0\ \mathrm{mm^2}=6.0\,(10^{-3}\ \mathrm m)^2=6.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^2}$$
$$90\ \mathrm{km/h}=90\cdot\frac{10^{3}\ \mathrm m}{3600\ \mathrm s}=25\ \mathrm{m/s}$$

*Trap:* Using $10^{3}$ where $10^{-3}$ belongs, or converting a length but not its square.

*Check:* A smaller unit must give a larger number, and an area factor is the square of the length factor.

name: Significant figures and error propagation
teach:
When you combine measured numbers and must decide how many digits the answer deserves, or how large its uncertainty is, start from the kind of operation. A product or quotient keeps the fewest significant figures of its inputs. A sum keeps the fewest decimal places. Leading zeros never count, and trailing zeros after a decimal point do. Independent uncertainties add in quadrature, while a worst-case estimate adds them directly. Round only the final result.
$$z=x+y:\ \delta z=\sqrt{\delta x^{2}+\delta y^{2}}$$
$$z=xy:\ \frac{\delta z}{z}=\sqrt{\left(\frac{\delta x}{x}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{\delta y}{y}\right)^{2}}$$
$$z=x^{n}:\ \frac{\delta z}{z}=|n|\,\frac{\delta x}{x},\qquad \text{worst case for }xy:\ \frac{\delta z}{z}=\frac{\delta x}{x}+\frac{\delta y}{y}$$

The core intuition here is that a result cannot be more precise than its least precise input. Extra digits claim precision the data never had. Squaring a quantity doubles its relative uncertainty.

*Example:* Multiply $6.20$ m by $2.5$ m, then add $10.0\pm0.3$ and $20.0\pm0.4$.
$$6.20\times2.5=15.5\ \Rightarrow\ 16\ \mathrm{m^2}\ \text{(two figures)}$$
$$\delta z=\sqrt{0.3^{2}+0.4^{2}}=0.5,\qquad z=30.0\pm0.5$$

*Trap:* Using the significant-figure rule for a sum, or adding independent uncertainties directly.

*Check:* The combined uncertainty is at least as big as the larger input uncertainty.

name: Dimensional analysis
teach:
When you must check an equation, or find which combination of variables could give a quantity, write every symbol in the base dimensions $M$, $L$ and $T$ for mass, length and time. Compare the exponents on both sides. For a guessed form $Q\propto a^{p}b^{q}$, equate the exponent of each base dimension and solve for $p$ and $q$.
$$[\mathrm{force}]=MLT^{-2},\quad[\mathrm{energy}]=ML^{2}T^{-2},\quad[\mathrm{pressure}]=ML^{-1}T^{-2}$$

The core intuition here is that both sides of a physical equation have the same dimensions, and only like dimensions can be added. Pure numbers such as $\tfrac12$ or $\pi$ carry none.

*Example:* Find how a pendulum period $P$ depends on length $\ell$ with $[\ell]=L$ and gravity $g$ with $[g]=LT^{-2}$.
$$P\propto \ell^{p}g^{q}:\quad L^{p+q}\,T^{-2q}=T^{1}\ \Rightarrow\ q=-\tfrac12,\ p=\tfrac12$$
$$P\propto\sqrt{\ell/g}$$

*Trap:* Expecting the method to give numerical factors such as $2\pi$, or confusing dimensions with units.

*Check:* Every term in a sum has the same dimensions, and each exponent matches on both sides.

name: Vector components and addition
teach:
When a vector comes as a magnitude and an angle, or several vectors must be added, resolve every vector into components. Add the $x$ parts, add the $y$ parts, then rebuild the magnitude. Here $\theta$ is measured from the $+x$ axis, counterclockwise.
$$A_x=A\cos\theta,\quad A_y=A\sin\theta,\quad A=\sqrt{A_x^{2}+A_y^{2}}$$

The core intuition here is that components along perpendicular axes are independent. Vector addition then becomes ordinary addition, one axis at a time.

*Example:* Add $\vec A$ of $14$ at $60^\circ$ and $\vec B$ of $3.5$ along $-x$.
$$\vec A=(7.0,\ 12.12),\quad \vec B=(-3.5,\ 0)\ \Rightarrow\ \vec R=(3.5,\ 12.12)$$
$$R=\sqrt{3.5^{2}+12.12^{2}}\approx 12.6$$

*Trap:* Using sine for the $x$ component when the angle is from the $x$ axis, or adding magnitudes instead of components.

*Check:* The sum is never longer than the sum of the magnitudes and never shorter than their difference.

name: Dot and cross products
teach:
When you need work, power, torque, magnetic force, or a direction perpendicular to two vectors, choose the dot or the cross product. The dot product is a scalar. The cross product is a vector whose direction follows the right-hand rule: fingers along $\vec A$ curl toward $\vec B$ and the thumb gives the direction. Swapping the order flips its sign.
$$\vec A\cdot\vec B=AB\cos\theta=A_xB_x+A_yB_y+A_zB_z$$
$$|\vec A\times\vec B|=AB\sin\theta,\qquad (\vec A\times\vec B)_z=A_xB_y-A_yB_x$$

The core intuition here is that the dot product measures how much one vector lies along another. The cross product measures how much they are perpendicular, and its direction is perpendicular to both.

*Example:* Take $\vec A=(2,1,0)$ and $\vec B=(1,3,0)$.
$$\vec A\cdot\vec B=2(1)+1(3)=5$$
$$(\vec A\times\vec B)_z=2(3)-1(1)=5\ \Rightarrow\ \vec A\times\vec B=5\,\hat k$$

*Trap:* Using sine for the dot product, cosine for the cross product, or treating $\vec A\times\vec B$ as equal to $\vec B\times\vec A$.

*Check:* Perpendicular vectors have zero dot product, and parallel vectors have zero cross product.

name: One-dimensional kinematics
teach:
When a body moves along a line with constant acceleration, list what you know among the initial speed $u$, final speed $v$, acceleration $a$, displacement $s$ and time $t$. Then pick the equation that contains those and the unknown, but not the fifth quantity. Fix one direction as positive and take every sign from it. Free fall has $a=-g$ with $g=9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ when up is positive.
$$v=u+at,\qquad s=ut+\tfrac12at^{2},\qquad v^{2}=u^{2}+2as$$

The core intuition here is that five quantities are tied by two independent relations. Any three known values fix the other two, and the right equation skips the quantity you neither know nor want.

*Example:* A car brakes from $15$ m/s with $a=-3.0$ m/s$^2$. Find the stopping distance, where $v=0$.
$$0=u^{2}+2as\ \Rightarrow\ s=-\frac{u^{2}}{2a}=\frac{225}{6.0}=37.5\ \mathrm m$$

*Trap:* Giving a positive $a$ to a slowing body, or using these equations when the acceleration changes.

*Check:* Distance is positive along the motion, and the speed must shrink while $a$ opposes $v$.

name: Projectile and 2D kinematics
teach:
When a projectile flies without air resistance, or any motion has constant acceleration in two directions, split $v_0$ into components. Use the vertical equation to find the time, then put that time into the horizontal equation. On level ground the range is the horizontal distance at landing.
$$x=v_0\cos\theta\;t,\qquad y=v_0\sin\theta\;t-\tfrac12gt^{2},\qquad g=9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$$
$$R=\frac{v_0^{2}\sin2\theta}{g}$$

The core intuition here is that horizontal and vertical motion are independent. They share only the time of flight.

*Example:* A ball leaves level ground at $25$ m/s and $30^\circ$. Find its range.
$$t=\frac{2v_0\sin\theta}{g}=\frac{2(25)(0.50)}{9.8}=2.55\ \mathrm s$$
$$R=(25\cos30^\circ)(2.55)\approx 55\ \mathrm m$$

*Trap:* Giving the projectile a horizontal acceleration, or using the full speed $v_0$ in the horizontal equation.

*Check:* At the top $v_y=0$. Range peaks at $45^\circ$ and is equal for $\theta$ and $90^\circ-\theta$.

name: Reading physics graphs
teach:
When you are given or asked for a position, velocity or acceleration graph against time, read slopes for the next quantity down and areas for the next one up. Area below the time axis counts negative. A zero crossing of $v$ means the body reverses.
$$v=\frac{dx}{dt}=\text{slope of }x\text{--}t,\qquad a=\frac{dv}{dt}=\text{slope of }v\text{--}t$$
$$\Delta x=\int v\,dt=\text{area under }v\text{--}t$$

The core intuition here is that slope is a derivative and area is an integral. Each graph therefore carries the next one down in its slope and the next one up in its area.

*Example:* A body speeds up uniformly from $0$ to $8.0$ m/s in $2.0$ s, then holds $8.0$ m/s for $5.0$ s.
$$a=\frac{8.0}{2.0}=4.0\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$$
$$\Delta x=\tfrac12(2.0)(8.0)+(8.0)(5.0)=8.0+40=48\ \mathrm m$$

*Trap:* Reading the height of a $v$--$t$ graph as displacement, or the height of an $x$--$t$ graph as speed.

*Check:* Slope units are the $y$ unit per $x$ unit, and area units are their product.

name: Order-of-magnitude estimation
teach:
When a quantity has no exact data and a power of ten is enough, break it into factors you can guess. Round each to one significant figure and convert units. Multiply, then take the nearest power of ten.
$$N\approx x_1x_2x_3,\qquad \text{answer}=10^{\,\mathrm{round}(\log_{10}N)}$$

The core intuition here is that factor-of-two errors in several rough inputs partly cancel. The order of magnitude therefore survives.

*Example:* Estimate the breaths a person takes in a day at about $15$ per minute.
$$N\approx 15\times60\times24=2.2\times10^{4},\qquad \log_{10}N=4.3\ \Rightarrow\ 10^{4}$$

*Trap:* Skipping a unit conversion, or rounding down a $\log_{10}$ that ends in $.7$.

*Check:* Compare with a familiar number of the same kind, such as the seconds in an hour.

name: Scaling and proportional reasoning
teach:
When one quantity depends on another as a power and you are asked what happens if the other changes by a factor, work with the ratio of the two cases. Find the exponent $n$ either from geometry, where length gives $1$, area $2$ and volume $3$, or from the law itself. Gravity falls with exponent $-2$ in distance, and a pendulum period grows with exponent $\tfrac12$ in length.
$$Q\propto x^{n}\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{Q_2}{Q_1}=\left(\frac{x_2}{x_1}\right)^{n}$$

The core intuition here is that the ratio of two cases depends only on the exponent. No constants or numerical values are needed.

*Example:* A planet's pull on a satellite follows $F\propto r^{-2}$, and the distance triples.
$$\frac{F_2}{F_1}=3^{-2}=\frac19$$

*Trap:* Using the ratio without the exponent, or flipping it when the exponent is negative.

*Check:* A positive exponent grows the result and a negative one shrinks it.

name: Small-quantity approximations
teach:
When an angle or a ratio is much smaller than $1$, as in a pendulum swing or a thin wedge, replace the function by its short series. The angle $\theta$ must be in radians, so convert degrees first with $\theta=\text{degrees}\times\pi/180$. A small object of size $d$ at distance $D$ also subtends the angle $d/D$ in radians.
$$\sin\theta\approx\tan\theta\approx\theta,\qquad \cos\theta\approx1-\frac{\theta^{2}}{2},\qquad (1+x)^{n}\approx1+nx$$
$$\theta\approx\frac{d}{D}$$

The core intuition here is that smooth functions are almost straight lines near zero, so a short series costs little error. It turns hard equations, such as the pendulum, into easy ones.

*Example:* Approximate $\sin$ and $\cos$ for $5^\circ$.
$$\theta=5\cdot\frac{\pi}{180}=0.0873\ \mathrm{rad}$$
$$\sin\theta\approx0.0873,\qquad \cos\theta\approx1-\frac{0.0873^{2}}{2}=0.9962$$

*Trap:* Putting a degree value straight into the approximation. The sine of $5$ is not close to $5$, because the rule only holds for radians.

*Check:* The error of $\sin\theta\approx\theta$ is about $\theta^{3}/6$, tiny here. Compare with a calculator once to see the size.

name: Linearizing data
teach:
When data should follow a power law or an exponential and you want a straight line to read a constant, pick the axes that make the law linear. The slope or intercept then gives the constant. For $y=kx^{2}$, plot $y$ against $x^{2}$.
$$y=kx^{n}\ \Rightarrow\ \log y=n\log x+\log k,\qquad y=Ae^{bx}\ \Rightarrow\ \ln y=bx+\ln A$$

The core intuition here is that a straight line is the one curve a ruler can fit and test. Choosing axes that turn the law into $y=mx+c$ puts the unknown constant in the slope.

*Example:* A pendulum obeys $T^{2}=(4\pi^{2}/g)\,L$, and a plot of $T^{2}$ against $L$ has slope $4.03\ \mathrm{s^2/m}$.
$$g=\frac{4\pi^{2}}{\text{slope}}=\frac{39.5}{4.03}\approx 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$$

*Trap:* Reading the slope of a curved plot, or taking the log-log slope as $k$ when it is $n$.

*Check:* The points lie on a straight line, and the slope has units of $y$ per $x$.

name: Calculus as rates and sums
teach:
When a problem asks for the rate of change at an instant, differentiate. When it asks for a total built up from a changing quantity, integrate between limits and subtract the lower limit from the upper.
$$\frac{d}{dt}t^{n}=nt^{n-1},\qquad \int t^{n}\,dt=\frac{t^{n+1}}{n+1}$$
$$v=\frac{dx}{dt},\qquad \Delta x=\int v\,dt,\qquad W=\int F\,dx$$

The core intuition here is that a derivative is the rate at one instant, and an integral adds up many small pieces. Each undoes the other.

*Example:* A body has $x=3t^{3}-2t$ metres. Find its speed at $t=2$ s, and $\int_0^3 2t^{2}\,dt$.
$$v=9t^{2}-2=9(4)-2=34\ \mathrm{m/s}$$
$$\int_0^3 2t^{2}\,dt=\frac{2t^{3}}{3}\Big|_0^3=18$$

*Trap:* Dropping the $1/(n+1)$ in an integral, or forgetting the lower limit.

*Check:* A derivative has units of the quantity per unit of the variable, and an integral has their product.

name: Newton's laws
teach:
Whenever the motion of an object is set by the forces on it, or you must find a force from a given motion, isolate one object and add the forces on it as vectors. Write one equation per axis. For touching bodies, treat them as one system to find $a$, then isolate one body for the contact force. Every force has a partner, equal and opposite, but it acts on the other body.
$$\sum\vec F=m\vec a$$

The core intuition here is that acceleration comes from the net force, not from any single force. With zero net force the velocity stays constant, so no force is needed to keep a body moving.

*Example:* A $5.0$ kg body feels $3.0$ N along $+x$ and $4.0$ N along $+y$.
$$a_x=\frac{3.0}{5.0}=0.60,\quad a_y=\frac{4.0}{5.0}=0.80\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$$
$$a=\sqrt{0.60^{2}+0.80^{2}}=1.0\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$$

*Trap:* Cancelling an action-reaction pair, which acts on two different bodies, or using one force instead of the net force.

*Check:* The acceleration points along the net force, and doubling the mass halves it.

name: Free-body diagrams
teach:
In any problem with forces on a body, whether it sits still or accelerates, start with a diagram of one chosen body. Draw weight $mg$ down, the normal force perpendicular to the surface, tension along the rope, and friction along the surface. Pick axes with one along the acceleration, then write the force sum for each axis.
$$\sum F_x=ma_x,\qquad \sum F_y=ma_y$$

The core intuition here is that most errors are a missing force or a force that does not exist. A diagram makes you list each real force once, with its direction.

*Example:* A $6.0$ kg block on a table is pulled by a rope with $25$ N at $37^\circ$ above horizontal. It stays on the table.
$$N+T\sin37^\circ-mg=0$$
$$N=(6.0)(9.8)-(25)(0.60)=44\ \mathrm N$$

*Trap:* Drawing a force of motion, or assuming the normal force always equals $mg$.

*Check:* The normal force cannot be negative. A negative value means the body has left the surface.

name: Friction and drag
teach:
When a body touches a surface, first compare the applied force with the static limit $\mu_sN$, where $N$ is the normal force. If the applied force is smaller, friction equals it and nothing moves. If it is larger, the body slides and kinetic friction $\mu_kN$ acts against the motion. In linear drag $F=-bv$ with drag constant $b$, the speed levels off at the terminal speed $v_t$, where the weight balances the drag.
$$f_s\le\mu_sN,\qquad f_k=\mu_kN,\qquad mg=bv_t\ \text{(linear drag)}$$

The core intuition here is that static friction adjusts to whatever is needed, up to a limit. Once sliding, kinetic friction has a fixed size, and drag grows with speed until it balances the weight.

*Example:* A $20$ kg box has $\mu_s=0.45$ and $\mu_k=0.35$. A $100$ N push is applied. Here $N=mg=196$ N.
$$\mu_sN=0.45(196)=88\ \mathrm N<100\ \mathrm N\ \Rightarrow\ \text{slides}$$
$$a=\frac{100-0.35(196)}{20}=1.6\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$$

*Trap:* Using $\mu_sN$ as the friction force before the body slips.

*Check:* Friction opposes the relative motion, and the box accelerates only if the push beats the limit.

name: Inclines, pulleys, constraints
teach:
For a block on a slope of angle $\theta$, tilt the axes so that one runs along the slope and one perpendicular to it, and let $\mu$ be the friction coefficient. For masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ hanging over a pulley, write $\sum F=ma$ for each mass. A massless frictionless pulley gives the same tension on both sides, and the rope gives both masses the same acceleration magnitude.
$$a=g\sin\theta-\mu g\cos\theta,\qquad N=mg\cos\theta$$
$$a=\frac{(m_1-m_2)g}{m_1+m_2}\quad\text{(Atwood machine)}$$

The core intuition here is that on a slope gravity splits into a part along the surface and a part into it. On a pulley the rope links the two accelerations and carries one tension.

*Example:* A block slides down a $37^\circ$ slope with $\mu_k=0.25$.
$$a=9.8\,(\sin37^\circ-0.25\cos37^\circ)=9.8\,(0.60-0.20)\approx3.9\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$$

*Trap:* Using cosine for the part along the slope, or giving each side of the pulley its own tension.

*Check:* With no friction the result is $g\sin\theta$, and friction only lowers it.

name: Circular motion
teach:
A body that follows a curved path at steady speed, such as a car on a bend or a satellite, accelerates toward the centre. Find the net force toward the centre and set it equal to $mv^{2}/r$, where $r$ is the radius, $\omega$ the angular speed and $P$ the period. On a flat curve friction supplies that force. On a frictionless bank of angle $\theta$, the normal force supplies it, and the last line follows.
$$a_c=\frac{v^{2}}{r}=\omega^{2}r,\qquad F_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{mv^{2}}{r},\qquad P=\frac{2\pi r}{v}=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}$$
$$v_{\max}=\sqrt{\mu_sgr}\ \text{(flat curve)},\qquad \tan\theta=\frac{v^{2}}{rg}\ \text{(frictionless bank)}$$

The core intuition here is that a changing direction means acceleration toward the centre. Some real force must supply it, so your job is to find which one.

*Example:* A flat curve has radius $30$ m and $\mu_s=0.60$.
$$v_{\max}=\sqrt{\mu_sgr}=\sqrt{0.60(9.8)(30)}\approx13\ \mathrm{m/s}$$

*Trap:* Adding an outward centrifugal force to the diagram of a body in an inertial frame.

*Check:* The required force grows as $v^{2}$ and falls as $r$ grows.

name: Work and kinetic energy
teach:
If a force acts through a distance, or you want a speed and have no time, find the work of each force using the angle between force and displacement. Add the works with signs and set the sum equal to the change in kinetic energy. For a variable force use $\int F\,dx$.
$$W=Fs\cos\theta,\qquad W_{\mathrm{net}}=\Delta K=\tfrac12m\left(v_f^{2}-v_i^{2}\right)$$

The core intuition here is that net work changes the kinetic energy. This skips the acceleration and the time entirely.

*Example:* A $5.0$ kg body starts from rest. A $40$ N force at $37^\circ$ to the motion acts over $5.0$ m. Use $\cos37^\circ\approx0.80$.
$$W=40(5.0)\cos37^\circ=160\ \mathrm J$$
$$v=\sqrt{\frac{2W}{m}}=\sqrt{\frac{320}{5.0}}=8.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$$

*Trap:* Using the whole force instead of its component along the motion.

*Check:* Positive net work speeds the body up, and negative net work slows it.

name: Potential energy and conservation
teach:
When only conservative forces such as gravity and springs do work, or a force comes from a potential energy, choose a zero for $U$. Write the total energy at the start and at the end, then solve for the unknown speed or height. Turning points are where $K=0$.
$$K_i+U_i=K_f+U_f,\qquad U_g=mgh,\qquad U_s=\tfrac12kx^{2},\qquad F=-\frac{dU}{dx}$$

The core intuition here is that energy leaving kinetic form is stored as potential and can come back. The path does not matter, only the end points.

*Example:* A spring with $k=120$ N/m is compressed $0.25$ m and launches a $0.30$ kg block along a frictionless floor.
$$\tfrac12(120)(0.25)^{2}=\tfrac12(0.30)v^{2}\ \Rightarrow\ v=5.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$$

*Trap:* Applying conservation when friction or another non-conservative force acts.

*Check:* Kinetic energy is never negative, so $U$ cannot exceed the total energy.

name: Momentum and impulse
teach:
In a collision, a brief push, or an isolated system where forces act over a short time, choose a positive direction and write the momentum before and after with signs. For an impulse, take final minus initial, then divide by the contact time for the average force.
$$\vec p=m\vec v,\qquad \vec J=\int\vec F\,dt=\Delta\vec p,\qquad \sum\vec p_{\mathrm{before}}=\sum\vec p_{\mathrm{after}}$$

The core intuition here is that a force acting for a time changes momentum. When the net external force is zero, the total momentum cannot change.

*Example:* A $0.25$ kg ball hits a wall at $14$ m/s and rebounds at $6.0$ m/s. Contact lasts $0.020$ s.
$$\Delta p=0.25\,\big(6.0-(-14)\big)=5.0\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}$$
$$F_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{5.0}{0.020}=250\ \mathrm N$$

*Trap:* Dropping the sign of a reversed velocity, which makes the change too small.

*Check:* The impulse points along the change in velocity, here away from the wall.

name: Collisions
teach:
When two bodies interact over a short time and you want their velocities afterwards, always write the momentum equation first. Then add a second condition: $e=1$ for an elastic hit, or $e=0$ when the bodies stick. For an elastic hit on a target at rest, use the closed forms below. In a ballistic pendulum, use momentum for the hit, then energy for the rise.
$$m_1u_1+m_2u_2=m_1v_1+m_2v_2,\qquad e=\frac{v_2-v_1}{u_1-u_2}$$
$$v_1=\frac{m_1-m_2}{m_1+m_2}\,u_1,\qquad v_2=\frac{2m_1}{m_1+m_2}\,u_1$$

The core intuition here is that internal forces cancel in pairs, so momentum survives every collision. Kinetic energy survives only if the bodies bounce perfectly.

*Example:* A $1.5$ kg cart at $8.0$ m/s hits a $2.5$ kg cart at rest and they stick.
$$v=\frac{1.5(8.0)}{1.5+2.5}=3.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$$
$$\Delta K=\tfrac12(4.0)(3.0)^{2}-\tfrac12(1.5)(8.0)^{2}=-30\ \mathrm J$$

*Trap:* Conserving kinetic energy in an inelastic collision.

*Check:* Kinetic energy after the collision is never larger than before.

name: Center of mass and two-body motion
teach:
For a system of several bodies, find the centre of mass by taking the mass-weighted average of their positions. It moves as one body of total mass $M$ pushed by the external forces alone. For two bodies that attract each other, the relative motion behaves like one body of reduced mass $\mu$ under their mutual force.
$$x_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{\sum m_ix_i}{\sum m_i},\qquad M\vec a_{\mathrm{cm}}=\sum\vec F_{\mathrm{ext}},\qquad \mu=\frac{m_1m_2}{m_1+m_2}$$

The core intuition here is that the centre of mass moves as if all the mass sat there and only external forces acted. Internal forces drop out.

*Example:* A $5.0$ kg mass sits at $x=0$ and a $15$ kg mass at $x=8.0$ m.
$$x_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{5.0(0)+15(8.0)}{20}=6.0\ \mathrm m,\qquad \mu=\frac{5.0(15)}{20}=3.75\ \mathrm{kg}$$

*Trap:* Counting internal forces in $\sum\vec F_{\mathrm{ext}}$.

*Check:* The centre of mass lies between the bodies and nearer the heavier one.

name: Torque and static equilibrium
teach:
To hold a rigid body still, or to see whether a force may turn it about a pivot, choose a pivot at an unknown force so that force drops out. Count torques counterclockwise positive. Solve the torque equation first, then the force equations.
$$\tau=rF\sin\theta,\qquad \sum\vec F=0,\qquad \sum\tau=0$$

The core intuition here is that a body stays at rest only if forces and turning effects both balance. A force's turning effect grows with its lever arm.

*Example:* A uniform $3.0$ m beam of $12$ kg is held horizontal by a hinge at a wall and a vertical rope at the far end.
$$T\,(3.0)=(12)(9.8)(1.5)\ \Rightarrow\ T=59\ \mathrm N$$

*Trap:* Using the full length instead of the perpendicular distance from the pivot, or forgetting that the weight acts at the centre.

*Check:* Any other pivot must give the same answer.

name: Rotational dynamics
teach:
When a body spins, rolls, or feels a torque about an axis, use the moment of inertia $I$ about that same axis. Rolling without slipping means the contact point is at rest, so $v=\omega R$. A string that does not slip on a pulley links the block's acceleration to the pulley's angular acceleration in the same way. For a rolling body with $I=cmR^{2}$, the last line gives the share of its kinetic energy that is rotational.
$$\tau=I\alpha,\qquad v=\omega R,\qquad a=\alpha R,\qquad K=\tfrac12mv^{2}+\tfrac12I\omega^{2}$$
$$I_{\mathrm{hoop}}=mR^{2},\quad I_{\mathrm{disk}}=\tfrac12mR^{2},\quad I_{\mathrm{sphere}}=\tfrac25mR^{2}$$
$$\frac{K_{\mathrm{rot}}}{K}=\frac{c}{1+c}$$

The core intuition here is that rotation follows the same law as straight-line motion. Torque takes the place of force, and moment of inertia takes the place of mass.

*Example:* A hoop of mass $3.0$ kg and radius $0.20$ m feels a torque of $0.60$ N m.
$$I=mR^{2}=3.0(0.20)^{2}=0.12\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2},\qquad \alpha=\frac{0.60}{0.12}=5.0\ \mathrm{rad/s^2}$$

*Trap:* Using $mR^{2}$ for every shape, or measuring $I$ about the wrong axis.

*Check:* The larger $I$ is, the smaller the angular acceleration for the same torque.

name: Angular momentum
teach:
If a spinning system changes shape, or collides, with no outside torque about its axis, write $L$ before and after and solve for the new $\omega$. First check that the external torque about the axis is zero. Energy is not conserved here.
$$\vec L=\vec r\times\vec p,\qquad L=I\omega=mvr\ \text{(point mass, tangential }v\text{)},\qquad I_1\omega_1=I_2\omega_2$$

The core intuition here is that angular momentum changes only through an external torque. Pulling mass inward must therefore raise the spin rate.

*Example:* A skater with $I=6.0$ kg m$^2$ spins at $1.5$ rad/s and pulls in her arms to $I=2.0$ kg m$^2$.
$$\omega_2=\frac{I_1\omega_1}{I_2}=\frac{6.0(1.5)}{2.0}=4.5\ \mathrm{rad/s}$$

*Trap:* Conserving kinetic energy as well. Here it rises from $6.8$ to $20$ J because her arms do work.

*Check:* A smaller $I$ means a faster spin.

name: Gravitation and Kepler
teach:
When a body orbits, or moves freely under the pull of a large mass $M$, set the gravitational force $GMm/r^{2}$ on the body of mass $m$ equal to the inward force its motion needs. Measure $r$ from the centre of the planet, not from the surface. Use $GM_E=3.98\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{m^3/s^2}$ and $R_E=6.37\times10^{6}$ m. At a planet's surface $GM=gR^{2}$, so $g$ falls as $1/r^{2}$ outside.
$$F=\frac{GMm}{r^{2}},\qquad v_{\mathrm{orb}}=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}},\qquad v_{\mathrm{esc}}=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}},\qquad T^{2}\propto r^{3}$$

The core intuition here is that gravity supplies the inward force of a circular orbit. Setting $GMm/r^{2}$ equal to $mv^{2}/r$ ties speed, radius and period together, and the satellite mass cancels.

*Example:* Find the circular orbital speed at $300$ km altitude.
$$r=6.37\times10^{6}+3.0\times10^{5}=6.67\times10^{6}\ \mathrm m$$
$$v=\sqrt{\frac{3.98\times10^{14}}{6.67\times10^{6}}}\approx7.7\ \mathrm{km/s}$$

*Trap:* Using the altitude as $r$, or taking $\sqrt{GM/R}$ for escape speed. The circular-orbit value is smaller than the escape value.

*Check:* Escape speed is $\sqrt2$ times the circular speed at the same radius.

name: Simple harmonic motion
teach:
Whenever a restoring force grows in proportion to the displacement, as for a spring of constant $k$ or a small-angle pendulum, find the angular frequency $\omega$ from the system. Read the amplitude $A$ from where the motion starts at rest. Energy then swaps between kinetic and potential.
$$\omega=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}},\qquad T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega},\qquad v_{\max}=A\omega,\qquad a_{\max}=A\omega^{2},\qquad E=\tfrac12kA^{2}$$
$$\omega_{\mathrm{pendulum}}=\sqrt{\frac{g}{L}}$$

The core intuition here is that a force $-kx$ gives acceleration $-(k/m)x$. The solution is a sinusoid with a frequency fixed by $k$ and $m$, not by the amplitude.

*Example:* A $0.80$ kg mass on a $20$ N/m spring is pulled $0.15$ m and released.
$$\omega=\sqrt{\frac{20}{0.80}}=5.0\ \mathrm{rad/s},\qquad T=\frac{2\pi}{5.0}=1.26\ \mathrm s$$
$$v_{\max}=0.15(5.0)=0.75\ \mathrm{m/s}$$

*Trap:* Thinking the period depends on amplitude, or putting $g$ into the spring formula.

*Check:* A stiffer spring or a lighter mass gives a shorter period.

name: Damped and driven oscillators
teach:
If an oscillator loses energy to drag, or is pushed at some driving frequency, find the decay time and the damped frequency first. The drag force is $-bv$, the natural frequency is $\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}$, and the driving force has amplitude $F$ and frequency $\omega$. The amplitude decays as $e^{-t/\tau}$, while the energy decays twice as fast.
$$x=Ae^{-t/\tau}\cos\omega_dt,\qquad \tau=\frac{2m}{b},\qquad \omega_d=\sqrt{\omega_0^{2}-\left(\frac{b}{2m}\right)^{2}},\qquad Q=\frac{\omega_0m}{b}$$
$$A_{\mathrm{driven}}=\frac{F}{\sqrt{m^{2}(\omega_0^{2}-\omega^{2})^{2}+b^{2}\omega^{2}}},\qquad A_{\mathrm{res}}=\frac{F}{b\,\omega_0}$$

The core intuition here is that damping drains the amplitude exponentially. Driving at the natural frequency feeds energy in at the best moment, so the response peaks.

*Example:* A $3.0$ kg mass on a $48$ N/m spring has $b=0.60$ kg/s. Find the amplitude fraction after $20$ s, then $Q$, then the resonant amplitude for $F=2.4$ N.
$$\tau=\frac{2m}{b}=10\ \mathrm s,\qquad \frac{A}{A_0}=e^{-20/10}=0.14,\qquad \omega_0=4.0\ \mathrm{rad/s}$$
$$Q=\frac{4.0(3.0)}{0.60}=20,\qquad A_{\mathrm{res}}=\frac{2.4}{0.60(4.0)}=1.0\ \mathrm m$$

*Trap:* Using $m/b$ for the amplitude decay time. That is the decay time of the energy.

*Check:* Amplitude falls by $e$ every $\tau$. Light damping leaves $\omega_d\approx\omega_0$, and $Q=\omega_0\tau/2$.

name: Wave properties
teach:
Suppose a periodic disturbance travels along a string, through air, or through any medium, and you need its speed, frequency or wavelength. Find the speed $v$ from the medium, then use $v=f\lambda$ for the unknown. On a string, $F$ is the tension and $\mu$ the mass per length. Here $T$ is the period, $k$ the wavenumber, and $\Delta\varphi$ the phase difference between two points $\Delta x$ apart.
$$v=f\lambda=\frac{\omega}{k},\quad f=\frac1T,\quad \omega=2\pi f,\quad k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda},\quad v_{\mathrm{string}}=\sqrt{\frac{F}{\mu}},\quad \Delta\varphi=k\,\Delta x$$

The core intuition here is that each crest advances one wavelength per period, so speed, frequency and wavelength are tied together. The medium sets the speed, and the source sets the frequency.

*Example:* A string under $90$ N tension has $\mu=0.010$ kg/m. It is driven at $150$ Hz.
$$v=\sqrt{\frac{90}{0.010}}=95\ \mathrm{m/s},\qquad \lambda=\frac{v}{f}=\frac{95}{150}=0.63\ \mathrm m$$

*Trap:* Believing a faster source makes a faster wave. Speed stays fixed, so the wavelength shrinks instead.

*Check:* Raising the frequency in the same medium shortens the wavelength.

name: Superposition and standing waves
teach:
Where two waves overlap, add their displacements point by point. For two equal waves that differ in phase by $\varphi$, the resultant amplitude follows from the first line. A string fixed at both ends has a node at each end, so only whole numbers of half wavelengths fit, with $n=1,2,3,\dots$
$$y=y_1+y_2,\qquad A_{\mathrm{res}}=2A\cos\frac{\varphi}{2},\qquad \lambda_n=\frac{2L}{n},\qquad f_n=\frac{nv}{2L}$$

The core intuition here is that overlapping waves simply add their displacements. Reflections at the ends of a string trap the pattern into fixed nodes.

*Example:* A $0.60$ m string with wave speed $120$ m/s is fixed at both ends. Find its first and third resonances. Separately, two equal waves differ in phase by $120^\circ$.
$$f_1=\frac{120}{2(0.60)}=100\ \mathrm{Hz},\qquad f_3=300\ \mathrm{Hz}$$
$$A_{\mathrm{res}}=2A\cos60^\circ=A$$

*Trap:* Adding intensities instead of amplitudes, or putting an antinode at a fixed end.

*Check:* The resultant amplitude lies between $0$ and $2A$.

name: Sound and the Doppler effect
teach:
When a source or listener moves through air, or air resonates in a pipe, take $v=343$ m/s unless told otherwise. Count $v_L$ positive when the listener moves toward the source and $v_S$ positive when the source moves toward the listener. Two close frequencies beat at their difference. In the pipe formulas $k=1,2,\dots$
$$f'=f\,\frac{v+v_L}{v-v_S},\qquad f_n=\frac{nv}{2L}\ \text{(open)},\qquad f=\frac{(2k-1)v}{4L}\ \text{(closed)},\qquad f_{\mathrm{beat}}=|f_1-f_2|$$

The core intuition here is that motion toward the listener squeezes the waves together, so the pitch rises, and motion away stretches them. A pipe's open or closed ends decide which standing waves fit.

*Example:* A $450$ Hz siren moves away from a still listener at $20$ m/s, so $v_S=-20$.
$$f'=450\cdot\frac{343}{343-(-20)}=450\cdot\frac{343}{363}=425\ \mathrm{Hz}$$

*Trap:* Getting the signs backwards, or expecting a closed pipe to sound even harmonics.

*Check:* Approach gives a higher pitch than the emitted one, and recession a lower one.

name: Intensity and decibels
teach:
If sound spreads from a point source, or sound levels must be compared or combined, compute intensities in $\mathrm{W/m^2}$ first. Add intensities, not decibels. A factor of $10$ in intensity is $10$ dB, and a factor of $2$ is about $3$ dB.
$$I=\frac{P}{4\pi r^{2}},\qquad \beta=10\log_{10}\frac{I}{I_0},\qquad I_0=10^{-12}\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$$

The core intuition here is that the same power spreads over a sphere whose area grows as $r^{2}$. The ear responds to ratios, so levels use a logarithm.

*Example:* A $0.50$ W source radiates evenly. Find the level at $2.0$ m.
$$I=\frac{0.50}{4\pi(2.0)^{2}}=0.010\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$$
$$\beta=10\log_{10}\frac{0.010}{10^{-12}}=100\ \mathrm{dB}$$

*Trap:* Adding two sound levels in decibels directly, or forgetting the square in the distance law.

*Check:* Doubling the distance lowers the level by about $6$ dB.

name: Reflection and refraction
teach:
Whenever light crosses the boundary between two media, or reflects from a surface, measure all angles from the normal. Reflection obeys $\theta_r=\theta_i$. Total internal reflection needs light going toward the lower index at an angle above $\theta_c$.
$$n_1\sin\theta_1=n_2\sin\theta_2,\qquad n=\frac cv,\qquad \sin\theta_c=\frac{n_2}{n_1}\ (n_1>n_2),\qquad d_{\mathrm{app}}=d\,\frac{n_2}{n_1}\ \text{(seen from the }n_2\text{ side, near normal)}$$

The core intuition here is that frequency stays the same across a boundary but speed changes, so the wave front bends. Going into a slower medium bends it toward the normal.

*Example:* Light enters water, $n=1.33$, from air at $40^\circ$.
$$\sin\theta_2=\frac{\sin40^\circ}{1.33}=\frac{0.643}{1.33}=0.483\ \Rightarrow\ \theta_2=29^\circ$$

*Trap:* Measuring angles from the surface, or expecting total internal reflection into a denser medium.

*Check:* The ray bends toward the normal in the denser medium, so $\theta_2<\theta_1$.

name: Mirrors and thin lenses
teach:
To place the image that a mirror or thin lens forms of an object, apply the lens and mirror formula with careful signs. Converging lenses and concave mirrors have $f>0$, while diverging lenses and convex mirrors have $f<0$. A real object has $d_o>0$. A real image has $d_i>0$ and is inverted, and a virtual image has $d_i<0$ and is upright. Here $m$ is the magnification, $R$ the mirror radius, and $P$ the lens power, in dioptres when $f$ is in metres.
$$\frac1f=\frac1{d_o}+\frac1{d_i},\qquad m=-\frac{d_i}{d_o},\qquad f_{\mathrm{mirror}}=\frac R2,\qquad P=\frac1f$$

The core intuition here is that the formula links where the object is to where the image forms. The signs then tell you whether the image is real or virtual.

*Example:* A converging lens has $f=15$ cm and the object is at $20$ cm.
$$\frac1{d_i}=\frac1{15}-\frac1{20}=\frac1{60}\ \Rightarrow\ d_i=60\ \mathrm{cm}$$
$$m=-\frac{60}{20}=-3$$

*Trap:* Mixing signs, or forgetting the minus in the magnification.

*Check:* An object inside the focal length of a converging lens gives a virtual, upright, larger image.

name: Two-source interference
teach:
When two coherent sources, or two paths from one source, meet at a point, find the path difference $\Delta$ and express it in wavelengths. A whole number $m$ of wavelengths means bright, and a half-integer means dark. For two slits a distance $d$ apart, $\Delta=d\sin\theta$. For small angles on a screen at distance $L$, the fringe spacing is $\Delta y$.
$$\Delta=d\sin\theta,\qquad \Delta=m\lambda\ \text{(bright)},\qquad \Delta=\left(m+\tfrac12\right)\lambda\ \text{(dark)},\qquad \Delta y=\frac{\lambda L}{d},\qquad \varphi=\frac{2\pi\Delta}{\lambda}$$

The core intuition here is that waves arriving in step add, and waves arriving half a cycle apart cancel. The path difference decides which.

*Example:* Light of $500$ nm passes slits $0.25$ mm apart onto a screen $1.5$ m away.
$$\Delta y=\frac{(500\times10^{-9})(1.5)}{0.25\times10^{-3}}=3.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm m$$

*Trap:* Using this formula for large angles, or confusing fringe spacing with fringe position.

*Check:* A narrower slit gap spreads the fringes wider.

name: Thin-film interference
teach:
For light reflecting from the two faces of a thin transparent layer such as a soap film or coating, count the phase flips first. A reflection off a higher index gives a flip of $\pi$. Here $\lambda$ is the vacuum wavelength, $t$ the thickness and $n$ the film index. Reflection dark means transmission bright.
$$\text{one flip: bright }2nt=\left(m+\tfrac12\right)\lambda,\quad\text{dark }2nt=m\lambda$$
$$\text{zero or two flips: bright }2nt=m\lambda,\quad\text{dark }2nt=\left(m+\tfrac12\right)\lambda$$

The core intuition here is that the two reflected rays differ by the round-trip path in the film, plus a possible half-cycle shift at each surface.

*Example:* A soap film in air has $n=1.33$. Find its thinnest thickness that reflects $560$ nm brightly.
$$\text{one flip: }2nt=\tfrac12\lambda\ \Rightarrow\ t=\frac{560}{4(1.33)}=105\ \mathrm{nm}$$

*Trap:* Skipping the phase flips, or using the vacuum wavelength without the factor $n$.

*Check:* Changing the number of flips swaps bright and dark.

name: Diffraction and gratings
teach:
When light passes a single slit, an opening or a grating, find the angles from the order $m=1,2,\dots$ Here $a$ is the slit width, $d$ the line spacing and $N$ the lines per metre. For a grating the largest order is below $d/\lambda$ because $\sin\theta\le1$.
$$a\sin\theta=m\lambda\ \text{(single-slit dark)},\qquad d\sin\theta=m\lambda\ \text{(grating bright)},\qquad d=\frac1N$$

The core intuition here is that each point of an opening acts as a source. Their sum cancels at angles where the edges are out of step by whole wavelengths, and a grating sharpens the bright orders.

*Example:* A grating has $400$ lines/mm. Use $\lambda=550$ nm.
$$d=\frac1{4.0\times10^{5}}=2.5\ \mu\mathrm m,\qquad \sin\theta_1=\frac{0.55}{2.5}=0.22\ \Rightarrow\ \theta_1=13^\circ$$
$$\frac d\lambda=4.5\ \Rightarrow\ m_{\max}=4$$

*Trap:* Using the slit width $a$ in the grating formula, or counting an order at exactly $90^\circ$.

*Check:* Longer wavelengths diffract to larger angles.

name: Polarization
teach:
When light meets a polarizer, treat unpolarized light at the first ideal polarizer separately, because it passes exactly half the intensity. After that, each polarizer multiplies the intensity by $\cos^{2}\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between successive axes. When light reflects from a surface, it is fully polarized at Brewster's angle $\theta_B$.
$$I_1=\tfrac12I_0\ \text{(unpolarized)},\qquad I=I_0\cos^{2}\theta,\qquad \tan\theta_B=\frac{n_2}{n_1}$$

The core intuition here is that a polarizer passes only the field component along its axis. Intensity goes as the square of that component.

*Example:* Unpolarized light of intensity $I_0$ passes two polarizers whose axes are $20^\circ$ apart.
$$I=\tfrac12I_0\cos^{2}20^\circ=\tfrac12I_0\,(0.883)=0.44\,I_0$$

*Trap:* Applying $\cos^{2}\theta$ to unpolarized light at the first polarizer, or using $\cos\theta$ for the intensity when it belongs to the field.

*Check:* Crossed axes at $90^\circ$ pass nothing, and the result never exceeds the intensity that entered the last polarizer.

name: Optical instruments
teach:
When you work with a magnifier, microscope or telescope, take the angular magnification from the focal lengths. The near point is $N=25$ cm, $m_o$ is the objective magnification, and $f_o$ and $f_e$ are the objective and eyepiece focal lengths. A magnifier with the image at the near point gains one more unit. A telescope in normal adjustment has its image at infinity. The smallest resolvable angle uses the aperture diameter $D$ in the Rayleigh formula.
$$M=\frac Nf\ \text{(image at infinity)},\quad M=1+\frac Nf\ \text{(image at }N\text{)},\quad M_{\mathrm{tel}}=\frac{f_o}{f_e},\quad M_{\mathrm{micro}}=m_o\frac{N}{f_e},\quad L=f_o+f_e,\quad \theta_{\min}=1.22\frac{\lambda}{D}$$

The core intuition here is that an instrument raises the angle an object subtends at the eye. Diffraction at the aperture sets the finest detail that can be separated.

*Example:* A telescope has $f_o=90$ cm and $f_e=3.0$ cm, with a $0.12$ m aperture. Use $\lambda=500$ nm.
$$M=\frac{90}{3.0}=30,\qquad L=93\ \mathrm{cm}$$
$$\theta_{\min}=\frac{1.22(500\times10^{-9})}{0.12}=5.1\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{rad}$$

*Trap:* Using the sum of focal lengths for the magnification, or the difference for the length.

*Check:* A larger aperture resolves finer detail.

name: Fluid statics
teach:
When a fluid is at rest, find the pressure at depth $h$ from the first formula, with $p_0=1.01\times10^{5}$ Pa for the atmosphere and $\rho=1000$ kg/m$^3$ for water. For a body that floats, the weight equals the buoyant force $F_b$, so the submerged fraction of its volume is $\rho_{\mathrm{body}}/\rho_f$, where $V_{\mathrm{sub}}$ is the submerged volume.
$$p=p_0+\rho gh,\qquad F_b=\rho_fV_{\mathrm{sub}}\,g$$

The core intuition here is that the fluid at any depth supports the column above it. A submerged body displaces fluid, and the fluid pushes up with the weight of what was displaced.

*Example:* Find the submerged fraction of a block of density $750$ kg/m$^3$ floating in water. Then find the gauge pressure at $6.0$ m depth.
$$\frac{V_{\mathrm{sub}}}{V}=\frac{750}{1000}=0.75$$
$$p_{\mathrm{gauge}}=1000(9.8)(6.0)=5.9\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{Pa}$$

*Trap:* Using the whole body volume for buoyancy, or mixing absolute and gauge pressure.

*Check:* Absolute pressure is the gauge value plus about $10^{5}$ Pa.

name: Fluid dynamics
teach:
When an incompressible fluid flows steadily through a pipe, or leaves a tank through a hole, use continuity first to get the speeds, since the volume flow rate $Q=Av$ is the same at every cross-section. Then write Bernoulli between two points on the same streamline and solve for pressure or height. For a hole a depth $h$ below the surface, the jet speed is $\sqrt{2gh}$.
$$A_1v_1=A_2v_2=Q,\qquad p+\tfrac12\rho v^{2}+\rho gh=\text{const},\qquad v_{\mathrm{jet}}=\sqrt{2gh}$$

The core intuition here is that what flows in must flow out, so a narrower pipe is faster. Faster fluid carries more kinetic energy, paid for by lower pressure.

*Example:* Water at $1.0$ m/s in a pipe of radius $3.0$ cm enters a section of radius $1.0$ cm. Find the speed there and the pressure drop.
$$v_2=v_1\frac{A_1}{A_2}=1.0\cdot9=9.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$$
$$p_1-p_2=\tfrac12(1000)(9.0^{2}-1.0^{2})=4.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{Pa}$$

*Trap:* Using the radius ratio instead of the area ratio, or applying Bernoulli across a pump or friction.

*Check:* Where the fluid is faster, the pressure is lower.

name: Ideal gas and heat basics
teach:
For a fixed amount of gas, convert the temperature to kelvin first by adding $273$. Then use $pV=nRT$ for pressure, volume or temperature, where $n$ is the amount in moles, and use the molecular formulas for energy and speed, where $m$ is the mass of one molecule. Take $R=8.31$ J/(mol K) and $k_B=1.38\times10^{-23}$ J/K. At fixed volume, $p\propto T$.
$$pV=nRT,\qquad \bar K=\tfrac32k_BT,\qquad v_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{3k_BT}{m}}$$

The core intuition here is that pressure comes from molecules hitting the walls. Hotter molecules move faster and hit harder, so pressure rises with temperature.

*Example:* $3.0$ mol of gas at $77^\circ$C sits in $0.040$ m$^3$.
$$p=\frac{nRT}{V}=\frac{3.0(8.31)(350)}{0.040}\approx2.2\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$$
$$\bar K=\tfrac32(1.38\times10^{-23})(350)=7.2\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm J$$

*Trap:* Putting the temperature in Celsius, or mixing litres and cubic metres. Use SI units throughout so the pressure comes out in pascals.

*Check:* Doubling the kelvin temperature at fixed volume doubles the pressure. Room temperature gives a pressure near atmospheric for a mole in about $0.025$ m$^3$.

name: Coulomb's law and electric field
teach:
To get the force between point charges, or the electric field of one or several of them, take the size from the first formula and the direction from the signs. Like charges repel and unlike attract. For several charges, add the field vectors by components. Here $k=1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)=8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}$, with $\varepsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}$ F/m.
$$F=k\frac{|q_1q_2|}{r^{2}},\qquad E=k\frac{|Q|}{r^{2}},\qquad \vec F=q\vec E$$

The core intuition here is that charges push or pull along the line joining them with a strength that falls as $1/r^{2}$. Field is just force per unit test charge.

*Example:* Find the field $0.20$ m from an $8.0$ nC point charge, then the force on a $3.0\ \mu$C charge there.
$$E=\frac{(8.99\times10^{9})(8.0\times10^{-9})}{(0.20)^{2}}=1.8\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{N/C}$$
$$F=qE=(3.0\times10^{-6})(1.8\times10^{3})=5.4\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm N$$

*Trap:* Adding magnitudes of field instead of vectors, or forgetting to square $r$.

*Check:* Doubling the distance cuts the force to a quarter.

name: Gauss's law
teach:
When the charge has line, plane or sphere symmetry, the field has the same size everywhere on a surface that matches the symmetry. Choose that surface so that $E$ is constant or zero on every piece. Evaluate its area, find the charge inside, and solve for $E$. Only enclosed charge counts. For a uniform volume density $\rho$, the enclosed charge is $\rho$ times the enclosed volume, and $\sigma$ is the surface charge density.
$$\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A=\frac{Q_{\mathrm{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad E_{\mathrm{sphere}}=\frac{Q_{\mathrm{enc}}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^{2}},\quad E_{\mathrm{plane}}=\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$$

The core intuition here is that field lines from enclosed charge must pass through any closed surface around it. With symmetry the surface integral becomes simply $E$ times area.

*Example:* An infinite line carries $\lambda=3.5\ \mu$C/m. Find $E$ at $r=0.80$ m with a cylinder of length $\ell$.
$$E\,(2\pi r\ell)=\frac{\lambda\ell}{\varepsilon_0}\ \Rightarrow\ E=\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0r}$$
$$E=\frac{3.5\times10^{-6}}{2\pi(8.85\times10^{-12})(0.80)}=7.9\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{N/C}$$

*Trap:* Using the law without enough symmetry, or counting charge outside the surface.

*Check:* The result must fall as $1/r$ for a line and match $kQ/r^{2}$ for a sphere.

name: Electric potential
teach:
When you want energy per charge, or must convert between field and potential, take $V=0$ at infinity. Add the potentials of several charges with their signs, since negative charges give negative potential. A charge $q$ released from rest gains kinetic energy equal to the potential energy it loses, so the last formula applies with $V_i$ the starting and $V_f$ the final potential.
$$V=\frac{kQ}{r},\qquad \vec E=-\nabla V,\qquad U=qV,\qquad K_f=q\,(V_i-V_f)$$

The core intuition here is that potential is a scalar, so adding sources is easy. The field points downhill and is the slope of the potential.

*Example:* A $3.0$ nC and a $-1.0$ nC charge each sit $0.50$ m from a point.
$$V=\frac{(8.99\times10^{9})\,(3.0-1.0)\times10^{-9}}{0.50}=36\ \mathrm V$$

*Trap:* Treating potential as a vector, or dropping the sign of a negative charge.

*Check:* Potential is positive near positive charge, and field lines run from high to low potential.

name: Dipoles and multipoles
teach:
Two equal and opposite charges $\pm q$ a small distance $d$ apart form a dipole, whether seen from far away or placed in an external field. The moment $\vec p$ points from the negative to the positive charge, and $\theta$ is measured from it. The far-field forms need $d\ll r$. An external field turns the dipole toward $\vec E$, so $U$ is lowest when they are parallel.
$$p=qd,\qquad \tau=pE\sin\theta,\qquad U=-\vec p\cdot\vec E$$
$$V=\frac{kp\cos\theta}{r^{2}},\qquad E_{\mathrm{axis}}=\frac{2kp}{r^{3}},\qquad E_{\mathrm{equator}}=\frac{kp}{r^{3}}$$

The core intuition here is that the two fields nearly cancel at a distance, leaving a weaker pattern. A field also twists a dipole to line it up.

*Example:* Charges $\pm3.0$ nC are $2.0$ mm apart, in a field of $5.0\times10^{3}$ N/C.
$$p=(3.0\times10^{-9})(2.0\times10^{-3})=6.0\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C\,m}$$
$$\tau_{\max}=pE=3.0\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{N\,m},\qquad U_{\min}=-pE=-3.0\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm J$$

*Trap:* Using the single-charge falloff, which is much slower than for a dipole.

*Check:* A dipole in a uniform field feels torque but no net force.

name: Conductors in electrostatics
teach:
Once the charges on a metal object have settled, the net charge sits on its surface and the field inside the metal is zero. The field just outside is perpendicular to the surface. A charge inside a cavity induces an equal and opposite charge on the cavity wall, so the outer surface holds the shell's net charge plus the enclosed charge. Joined conductors share one potential, so for spheres the charge is proportional to the radius.
$$E_{\mathrm{in}}=0,\qquad V=\text{const},\qquad E_{\mathrm{surface}}=\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad \sigma=\frac{Q}{4\pi R^{2}}$$

The core intuition here is that free charges move until the field inside vanishes. Anything else would keep them moving.

*Example:* An isolated metal sphere of radius $0.15$ m carries $6.0$ nC.
$$\sigma=\frac{6.0\times10^{-9}}{4\pi(0.15)^{2}}=2.1\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{C/m^2}$$
$$E_{\mathrm{surface}}=\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}=2.4\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{N/C},\qquad V=\frac{kQ}{R}=360\ \mathrm V$$

*Trap:* Using $\sigma/2\varepsilon_0$ for a conductor, or expecting a field inside the metal.

*Check:* The surface value must also equal $kQ/R^{2}$.

name: Method of images
teach:
A point charge $q$ near a grounded conducting plane calls for an imagined charge, whether you need the force, energy, field at the plane or induced charge. Place an image of charge $-q$ the same distance $d$ behind the plane. The force uses the distance $2d$ to the image. The energy is half the charge-image pair value, because the image moves with the charge. Here $\rho$ is the distance along the plane from the foot of the perpendicular.
$$q_{\mathrm{image}}=-q\ \text{at the mirror point},\qquad F=\frac{kq^{2}}{(2d)^{2}},\qquad U=-\frac{kq^{2}}{4d}$$
$$\sigma(\rho)=-\frac{qd}{2\pi\,(d^{2}+\rho^{2})^{3/2}},\qquad E_{\mathrm{foot}}=\frac{2kq}{d^{2}}$$

The core intuition here is that the induced charges on the plane are hard to find directly. One imagined charge reproduces $V=0$ on the plane and the true potential on the real side, so every field there comes out right.

*Example:* A $4.0$ nC charge sits $0.060$ m from a grounded plane. Find the force, and the work to pull it to infinity.
$$F=\frac{(8.99\times10^{9})(4.0\times10^{-9})^{2}}{(0.12)^{2}}=1.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm N$$
$$W=-U=\frac{(8.99\times10^{9})(4.0\times10^{-9})^{2}}{4(0.060)}=6.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm J$$

*Trap:* Using $d$ instead of $2d$ in the force, using the full pair energy for the work, or using the image to find fields behind the plane.

*Check:* The force is attractive, directed toward the plane.

name: Laplace's equation and boundaries
teach:
In a region with no charge and a known potential on its boundary, pick the form of $V$ that fits the geometry. Use the two boundary values to fix $a$ and $b$, then take $\vec E=-\nabla V$. To test a given $V$, check that its second derivatives sum to zero.
$$\nabla^{2}V=0,\qquad V=a+bx\ \text{(plates)},\qquad V=a+b\ln r\ \text{(cylinders)},\qquad V=a+\frac br\ \text{(spheres)}$$

The core intuition here is that with no charge the potential has no local peaks or dips, and one boundary condition fixes exactly one solution.

*Example:* Plates at $x=0$ and $x=0.050$ m are held at $0$ and $200$ V.
$$V=\frac{200}{0.050}x=4000x,\qquad E=-\frac{dV}{dx}=-4000\ \mathrm{V/m}$$
$$V(0.020)=80\ \mathrm V$$

*Trap:* Assuming a straight-line potential between cylinders or spheres, where the geometry bends it. Only parallel plates give a straight line.

*Check:* The value in the middle lies between the two boundary values, and the field is uniform for flat plates.

name: Capacitors
teach:
To find charge, voltage or stored energy for conductors separated by an insulator, reduce the network first, then step back out to find each part. In parallel the voltage is shared and the charges add. In series the charge is shared and the voltages add. Joining charged capacitors in parallel pools their charge, so the common voltage is the total charge over the total capacitance.
$$C=\frac QV,\qquad C=\frac{\varepsilon_0A}{d},\qquad C_{\parallel}=C_1+C_2,\qquad \frac1{C_s}=\frac1{C_1}+\frac1{C_2}$$

The core intuition here is that a capacitor stores charge in proportion to the voltage across it. Plates that are bigger or closer hold more.

*Example:* A $3.0\ \mu$F and a $12\ \mu$F capacitor are in series across $15$ V.
$$C_s=\frac{3.0\cdot12}{15}=2.4\ \mu\mathrm F,\qquad Q=C_sV=36\ \mu\mathrm C$$
$$V_1=\frac{36}{3.0}=12\ \mathrm V,\qquad V_2=\frac{36}{12}=3.0\ \mathrm V$$

*Trap:* Adding series capacitances directly, or giving each series part a different charge.

*Check:* The series value is smaller than the smallest capacitor.

name: Dielectrics
teach:
Once an insulator of dielectric constant $\kappa$ fills the gap of a capacitor, ask first what is held fixed. A battery fixes the voltage, so the charge grows. An isolated capacitor fixes the charge, so the voltage falls from $V_0$ to $V_0/\kappa$. Here $C_0$ and $E_0$ are the values with the gap empty.
$$C=\kappa C_0,\qquad E=\frac{E_0}{\kappa}\ \text{(fixed free charge)}$$

The core intuition here is that the insulator's molecules polarize and cancel part of the field, so the same charge needs less voltage.

*Example:* A $2.0\ \mu$F capacitor charged to $12$ V is disconnected, then filled with $\kappa=5.0$.
$$Q=24\ \mu\mathrm C,\qquad C=10\ \mu\mathrm F,\qquad V=\frac{Q}{C}=2.4\ \mathrm V$$

*Trap:* Keeping the voltage fixed after the battery is disconnected. Only the charge is then fixed, so the voltage must drop.

*Check:* With the battery attached, $V$ would stay at $12$ V and $Q$ would instead rise to $120\ \mu$C.

name: DC circuits
teach:
For resistors and sources in steady direct-current operation, combine to one resistor and find the current from the source. Then work back to the branch voltages. A real battery of emf $\mathcal E$ has internal resistance $r$, and $P$ is the power dissipated in a resistor.
$$V=IR,\qquad R_s=R_1+R_2,\qquad \frac1{R_p}=\frac1{R_1}+\frac1{R_2},\qquad V_{\mathrm{term}}=\mathcal E-Ir,\qquad P=IV=I^{2}R=\frac{V^{2}}{R}$$

The core intuition here is that current is the same through series parts and voltage is the same across parallel parts. That lets you shrink the network step by step.

*Example:* A $30$ V battery with $r=0.50\ \Omega$ drives $8.0\ \Omega$ in series with $20\ \Omega$ parallel to $5.0\ \Omega$.
$$R_p=\frac{20\cdot5.0}{25}=4.0\ \Omega,\qquad I=\frac{30}{8.0+4.0+0.50}=2.4\ \mathrm A$$
$$V_{\mathrm{term}}=30-2.4(0.50)=28.8\ \mathrm V$$

*Trap:* Splitting the current equally between unequal parallel branches.

*Check:* The parallel value is smaller than its smallest resistor.

name: Kirchhoff's rules
teach:
When a network has several loops or junctions that series and parallel reduction cannot simplify, label a current in each branch with a guessed direction. Write a junction equation, then loop equations, going across a resistor with the current as $-IR$. Solve. A negative answer means the true direction is opposite.
$$\sum I_{\mathrm{in}}=\sum I_{\mathrm{out}},\qquad \sum\Delta V=0\ \text{around a loop}$$

The core intuition here is that charge does not pile up at a junction, and energy per charge is single-valued around any closed loop.

*Example:* Branch 1 has $7.0$ V and $2.0\ \Omega$. Branch 2 has $1.0$ V and $2.0\ \Omega$. Both feed $3.0\ \Omega$, with $I_3=I_1+I_2$.
$$7.0-2.0I_1-3.0\,(I_1+I_2)=0,\qquad 1.0-2.0I_2-3.0\,(I_1+I_2)=0$$
$$5I_1+3I_2=7,\quad 3I_1+5I_2=1\ \Rightarrow\ I_1=2.0\ \mathrm A,\ I_2=-1.0\ \mathrm A$$
The branch 2 current runs against the guess.

*Trap:* Using the wrong sign across a source or resistor.

*Check:* Put the answers into a third loop equation to test them.

name: RC transients
teach:
When a capacitor charges or discharges through a resistor, find the time constant $\tau=RC$ first and measure the elapsed time in units of $\tau$. Here $V_0$ is the source voltage when charging, or the starting voltage when discharging. At $t=0$ an uncharged capacitor acts as a wire, so the current is $V_0/R$. After a few $\tau$ it acts as a gap. The current magnitude falls exponentially in both cases.
$$\tau=RC,\qquad V_C=V_0\left(1-e^{-t/\tau}\right)\ \text{(charging)},\qquad V_C=V_0e^{-t/\tau}\ \text{(discharging)},\qquad I=\frac{V_0}{R}e^{-t/\tau}$$
$$t=\tau\ln\frac{V_0}{V}\ \text{(discharge to }V\text{)},\qquad t=-\tau\ln\left(1-\frac{V}{V_0}\right)\ \text{(charge to }V\text{)}$$

The core intuition here is that charge cannot jump. The rate is proportional to what remains, which gives an exponential.

*Example:* A $4.0\ \mu$F capacitor discharges through $3.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ from $9.0$ V. Find $V_C$ at $24$ ms.
$$\tau=(3.0\times10^{3})(4.0\times10^{-6})=12\ \mathrm{ms}$$
$$V_C=9.0\,e^{-24/12}=9.0\,(0.135)=1.2\ \mathrm V$$

*Trap:* Letting the capacitor voltage jump at the switch, or using $RC$ in the wrong units.

*Check:* After one $\tau$ a charging capacitor reaches $63\%$ of the final value.

name: Conduction and resistivity
teach:
When you need conductivity, drift speed or wire resistance from microscopic quantities, first get the current density $J=I/A$ and then apply the Drude formulas. Here $n$ is the carrier density, $q$ the carrier charge, $m$ its mass and $\tau$ the mean time between collisions. Take $e=1.6\times10^{-19}$ C.
$$\sigma=\frac{nq^{2}\tau}{m},\qquad v_d=\frac{J}{nq}=\frac{q\tau}{m}E,\qquad J=\sigma E,\qquad R=\frac{L}{\sigma A}$$

The core intuition here is that free electrons accelerate between collisions. The average gain in velocity before a collision gives a small steady drift.

*Example:* A $3.0$ A current flows in a copper wire of cross-section $1.5\ \mathrm{mm^2}$, with $n=8.5\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$.
$$J=\frac{3.0}{1.5\times10^{-6}}=2.0\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{A/m^2}$$
$$v_d=\frac{2.0\times10^{6}}{(8.5\times10^{28})(1.6\times10^{-19})}=1.5\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m/s}$$

*Trap:* Thinking drift speed is the speed of the electrons themselves. It is far smaller than their random thermal speed, and the signal travels much faster than either.

*Check:* Doubling the cross-section halves the drift speed for the same current, and doubling the current doubles it.

name: Electrostatic energy and forces
teach:
To find the energy stored in a capacitor or an electric field, or the change after altering the capacitor, use $Q^{2}/2C$ when the charge is fixed and $\tfrac12CV^{2}$ when the voltage is fixed. After a change, compute the new stored energy and subtract.
$$U=\tfrac12QV=\tfrac12CV^{2}=\frac{Q^{2}}{2C},\qquad u=\tfrac12\varepsilon E^{2},\qquad \varepsilon=\kappa\varepsilon_0$$

The core intuition here is that building up charge against the existing field costs work. That work is stored in the field itself.

*Example:* A $5.0\ \mu$F capacitor is charged to $20$ V, disconnected, and filled with $\kappa=2.0$.
$$U_0=\tfrac12(5.0\times10^{-6})(20)^{2}=1.0\ \mathrm{mJ}$$
$$U=\frac{Q^{2}}{2\kappa C}=\frac{(1.0\times10^{-4})^{2}}{2(1.0\times10^{-5})}=0.50\ \mathrm{mJ}$$

*Trap:* Using $\tfrac12CV^{2}$ with the old voltage after the capacitor is isolated.

*Check:* The energy halves because the field pulls the dielectric in and does work.

name: Lorentz force and charged-particle motion
teach:
A charge moving through a magnetic field, alone or together with an electric field, feels a force you find with the right-hand rule, reversed for a negative charge. Here $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec v$ and $\vec B$. For motion perpendicular to $B$, set $qvB=mv^{2}/r$. Use $e=1.6\times10^{-19}$ C and $m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}$ kg.
$$\vec F=q\vec v\times\vec B,\qquad F=|q|vB\sin\theta,\qquad r=\frac{mv}{|q|B},\qquad T=\frac{2\pi m}{|q|B},\qquad v=\frac EB\ \text{(crossed fields)}$$

The core intuition here is that the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity. It turns the particle without changing its speed, so it does no work.

*Example:* An electron moves at $3.0\times10^{6}$ m/s perpendicular to a $2.0$ mT field.
$$r=\frac{(9.11\times10^{-31})(3.0\times10^{6})}{(1.6\times10^{-19})(2.0\times10^{-3})}=8.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm m$$

*Trap:* Saying the magnetic field speeds the particle up, or forgetting to flip the direction for a negative charge.

*Check:* A faster particle moves on a larger circle, and the period does not change.

name: Biot-Savart law
teach:
If a current makes a field and the geometry has no simple symmetry, such as a loop or an arc, add up the small field of each current piece. Use $\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T m/A. Here $d\vec\ell$ is the current element and $\hat r$ points from it to the field point. Symmetry often cancels all but one component, and the right-hand rule gives its direction. An arc of angle $\theta$ gives the fraction $\theta/2\pi$ of a full loop's field at the centre.
$$d\vec B=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\,\frac{I\,d\vec\ell\times\hat r}{r^{2}},\qquad B_{\mathrm{wire}}=\frac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r},\qquad B_{\mathrm{coil,\,centre}}=\frac{\mu_0NI}{2R},\qquad B_{\mathrm{arc,\,centre}}=\frac{\mu_0I\theta}{4\pi R}$$

The core intuition here is that each short piece of current adds a small field. The total is the vector sum of all the pieces.

*Example:* A coil of $N=20$ turns and radius $0.25$ m carries $2.0$ A in each turn.
$$B=\frac{\mu_0NI}{2R}=\frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(20)(2.0)}{2(0.25)}=1.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm T$$

*Trap:* Mixing up the distance $r$ from the element with the length $d\ell$.

*Check:* The field is stronger closer to the current and grows with $I$.

name: Ampere's law
teach:
When the current has enough symmetry that $B$ has constant size along a chosen loop, as for a long wire, a solenoid or a cable, draw a loop along a field line. Count only current through the loop's surface, with sign. Here $n$ is turns per metre. Inside a thick wire with uniform current, $I_{\mathrm{enc}}$ grows as the area enclosed.
$$\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec\ell=\mu_0I_{\mathrm{enc}},\qquad B_{\mathrm{wire}}=\frac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r},\qquad B_{\mathrm{sol}}=\mu_0nI$$

The core intuition here is that the circulating field around a loop is fixed by the current threading it. This is just as flux fixes enclosed charge in Gauss's law.

*Example:* A wire of radius $6.0$ mm carries $18$ A uniformly. Find $B$ at $r=3.0$ mm.
$$I_{\mathrm{enc}}=18\left(\frac{3.0}{6.0}\right)^{2}=4.5\ \mathrm A$$
$$B=\frac{\mu_0I_{\mathrm{enc}}}{2\pi r}=\frac{(2\times10^{-7})(4.5)}{3.0\times10^{-3}}=3.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm T$$

*Trap:* Using the whole current for a point inside the wire.

*Check:* At the surface the inside and outside formulas must agree.

name: Magnetic materials
teach:
When a solenoid or toroid is filled with a magnetic material, find $H$ from the current first, then multiply by $\mu_0\mu_r$. Diamagnets have small negative $\chi$, paramagnets small positive $\chi$, and ferromagnets large positive $\chi$.
$$H=nI,\qquad B=\mu H=\mu_0\mu_rH,\qquad \mu_r=1+\chi,\qquad \vec B=\mu_0\left(\vec H+\vec M\right)$$

The core intuition here is that the free current sets the field $H$ alone. The material then adds its own magnetization, which scales the result.

*Example:* A toroid has $n=400$ turns/m and $I=0.60$ A, with an iron core of $\mu_r=500$.
$$H=400(0.60)=240\ \mathrm{A/m}$$
$$B=(4\pi\times10^{-7})(500)(240)=0.15\ \mathrm T$$

*Trap:* Letting the core change $H$. Only the free current sets it, while the material changes only $B$ and $M$.

*Check:* The core multiplies the empty-space field by $\mu_r$, so here $B$ is $500$ times larger than without iron.

name: Faraday's law
teach:
Whenever the flux through a loop changes because the field, the area or the angle changes, or a conductor moves across a field, compute the flux and find its rate of change. Then multiply by the number of turns $N$. Use the minus sign only to find the direction, since the induced field opposes the change.
$$\mathcal E=-N\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt},\qquad \Phi_B=BA\cos\theta,\qquad \mathcal E=BLv$$

The core intuition here is that a changing flux induces an electric field around the loop. The induced current opposes the change, which is why energy is conserved.

*Example:* A coil has $80$ turns of area $0.015$ m$^2$. The field through it rises from $0$ to $0.30$ T in $0.060$ s.
$$|\mathcal E|=N\,A\,\frac{\Delta B}{\Delta t}=80(0.015)\frac{0.30}{0.060}=6.0\ \mathrm V$$

*Trap:* Forgetting the number of turns, or using the angle from the plane instead of from the normal.

*Check:* No change in flux means no EMF, however large the field is.

name: Inductance and Lenz's law
teach:
When a coil's current changes, or you want the energy stored in a coil, find the inductance $L$ from the geometry. The EMF depends on how fast the current changes, not on its size, while the energy depends on the present current. For two coils, $M$ is the mutual inductance, with a plus sign in the series formula when the two fluxes add.
$$\mathcal E=-L\frac{dI}{dt},\qquad L=\frac{N\Phi_B}{I},\qquad L_{\mathrm{sol}}=\frac{\mu_0N^{2}A}{\ell},\qquad U=\tfrac12LI^{2},\qquad L_{\mathrm{series}}=L_1+L_2\pm2M$$

The core intuition here is that a coil resists changes in its own current by inducing an opposing EMF. The energy it takes to build the current is stored in the magnetic field.

*Example:* A solenoid has $N=300$, $A=5.0\times10^{-4}$ m$^2$ and length $0.15$ m. It carries $2.0$ A.
$$L=\frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(300)^{2}(5.0\times10^{-4})}{0.15}=3.8\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm H$$
$$U=\tfrac12(3.8\times10^{-4})(2.0)^{2}=7.5\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm J$$

*Trap:* Thinking the EMF is large when the current is large. It is large when the current changes fast.

*Check:* The inductance grows as the square of the turn count.

name: RL and LC circuits
teach:
When a resistor and inductor are switched onto a source, find the time constant $\tau=L/R$ and work in units of $\tau$. Just after switching an inductor acts as an open circuit, and a long time later it acts as a wire. Half the final current is reached at $t=\tau\ln2$. When the source is removed instead, the current decays as $I_0e^{-t/\tau}$. An ideal inductor and capacitor keep their total energy constant, $\tfrac12LI^{2}+Q^{2}/2C$, and oscillate at $\omega_0$.
$$\tau=\frac LR,\qquad I=\frac{\mathcal E}{R}\left(1-e^{-t/\tau}\right),\qquad I=I_0e^{-t/\tau},\qquad \omega_0=\frac1{\sqrt{LC}}$$

The core intuition here is that an inductor makes current rise gradually, so the time scale is $L/R$. With no resistor, energy slides between field and capacitor forever.

*Example:* A $0.20$ H coil in series with $50\ \Omega$ is connected to $10$ V. Separately, an LC circuit uses $L=0.10$ H and $C=10\ \mu$F.
$$\tau=\frac{0.20}{50}=4.0\ \mathrm{ms},\qquad I_{\infty}=\frac{10}{50}=0.20\ \mathrm A$$
$$\omega_0=\frac1{\sqrt{(0.10)(1.0\times10^{-5})}}=1000\ \mathrm{rad/s}$$

*Trap:* Letting the inductor current jump at the switch. Only its voltage can jump.

*Check:* At $t=\tau$ the current reaches $63\%$ of its final value.

name: AC circuits and phasors
teach:
When a sinusoidal source of angular frequency $\omega=2\pi f$ drives a resistor, an inductor and a capacitor in series, find both reactances, then $|Z|$, then $I_{\mathrm{rms}}=V_{\mathrm{rms}}/|Z|$. Current lags voltage in an inductor and leads it in a capacitor, and the last formula in the second line gives the phase angle by which the voltage leads the current.
$$X_L=\omega L,\quad X_C=\frac1{\omega C},\quad |Z|=\sqrt{R^{2}+(X_L-X_C)^{2}},\quad V_{\mathrm{rms}}=\frac{V_0}{\sqrt2},\quad P=I_{\mathrm{rms}}^{2}R$$
$$\tan\varphi=\frac{X_L-X_C}{R}$$

The core intuition here is that inductors and capacitors oppose current by reactance, and they shift its phase by quarter cycles. A phasor diagram adds them as perpendicular vectors.

*Example:* $R=60\ \Omega$, $L=80$ mH and $C=6.25\ \mu$F at $\omega=1000$ rad/s, with $200$ V rms.
$$X_L=80\ \Omega,\quad X_C=160\ \Omega,\quad |Z|=\sqrt{60^{2}+80^{2}}=100\ \Omega$$
$$I_{\mathrm{rms}}=\frac{200}{100}=2.0\ \mathrm A,\qquad P=(2.0)^{2}(60)=2.4\times10^{2}\ \mathrm W$$

*Trap:* Adding $R$, $X_L$ and $X_C$ directly as if all were resistances, or mixing peak and rms values in the power formula.

*Check:* The impedance is never smaller than $R$.

name: Resonance and filters
teach:
If a series RLC circuit is driven near its natural frequency, look for the frequency where $X_L=X_C$. There $|Z|=R$ and the current is in phase with the voltage. The frequency in hertz is $f_0=\omega_0/2\pi$, and the band narrows as $Q$ rises. A filter is a related case. An RC low-pass filter takes its output across $C$ and passes frequencies below the cutoff $\omega_c$.
$$\omega_0=\frac1{\sqrt{LC}},\qquad Q=\frac{\omega_0L}{R},\qquad \Delta\omega=\frac RL,\qquad \omega_c=\frac1{RC},\qquad |H|=\frac1{\sqrt{1+(\omega RC)^{2}}}$$

The core intuition here is that at resonance the inductor and capacitor effects cancel, leaving only the resistor. The current then peaks.

*Example:* A series circuit has $R=10\ \Omega$, $L=0.050$ H and $C=2.0\ \mu$F.
$$\omega_0=\frac1{\sqrt{(0.050)(2.0\times10^{-6})}}=3.2\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{rad/s}$$
$$Q=\frac{(3162)(0.050)}{10}=16,\qquad \Delta\omega=\frac{10}{0.050}=200\ \mathrm{rad/s}$$

*Trap:* Expecting the peak at a frequency set by $R$, or thinking a larger $R$ sharpens the peak.

*Check:* A larger resistance lowers $Q$ and widens the band.

name: Maxwell's equations
teach:
When fields vary in time, or you need the laws that link fields to charge and current, read each equation as one statement. Charge is the source of $\vec E$. There are no magnetic monopoles. A changing $\vec B$ curls $\vec E$. Current and a changing $\vec E$ curl $\vec B$. In empty space the two curl equations combine into a wave that moves at $c$.
$$\nabla\cdot\vec E=\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad \nabla\cdot\vec B=0$$
$$\nabla\times\vec E=-\frac{\partial\vec B}{\partial t},\qquad \nabla\times\vec B=\mu_0\vec J+\mu_0\varepsilon_0\frac{\partial\vec E}{\partial t}$$
$$\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec\ell=-\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt},\qquad \oint\vec B\cdot d\vec\ell=\mu_0\left(I+\varepsilon_0\frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}\right),\qquad c=\frac1{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}$$

The core intuition here is that four equations cover all of classical electromagnetism. Maxwell added the changing-field term to the last one, so a changing electric field also makes a magnetic field.

*Example:* A uniform field along the axis of a circular region rises at $0.50$ T/s. Find the induced $E$ at radius $r=0.10$ m, inside the region.
$$E\,(2\pi r)=\pi r^{2}\,\frac{dB}{dt}\ \Rightarrow\ E=\frac r2\,\frac{dB}{dt}=\frac{0.10}{2}(0.50)=0.025\ \mathrm{V/m}$$

*Trap:* Omitting the displacement term from the last equation, which makes waves impossible.

*Check:* Inside the region $E$ grows in proportion to $r$, and outside it falls as $1/r$.

name: Displacement current
teach:
While a capacitor is charging or discharging, no conduction current crosses the gap. Compute the flux of $\vec E$ through the surface, differentiate it, and multiply by $\varepsilon_0$. By continuity this equals the wire current $I$.
$$I_d=\varepsilon_0\frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}=\varepsilon_0A\frac{dE}{dt},\qquad J_d=\varepsilon_0\frac{\partial E}{\partial t}$$

The core intuition here is that a changing electric field acts like a current in Ampère's law. Without it, the law gives different answers for surfaces that bulge through the gap.

*Example:* Plates of area $0.020$ m$^2$ have a field changing at $5.0\times10^{9}$ V/(m s).
$$I_d=(8.85\times10^{-12})(0.020)(5.0\times10^{9})=8.9\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm A$$

*Trap:* Dropping the displacement current when the surface passes through the gap.

*Check:* The displacement current in the gap must equal the current in the wires.

name: Electromagnetic waves
teach:
For a plane wave in vacuum, start from $c=3.00\times10^{8}$ m/s and from the fact that $\vec E$ and $\vec B$ are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel. They peak together, and $\vec E\times\vec B$ gives the direction of propagation. Use $c=f\lambda$ to link frequency and wavelength, and $E_0=cB_0$ to convert between the fields. The cosine form describes a wave moving along $+z$ with its maximum at the origin.
$$c=\frac1{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}=f\lambda,\qquad E_0=cB_0,\qquad I=\tfrac12\varepsilon_0cE_0^{2}$$
$$E_x=E_0\cos(kz-\omega t),\qquad k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda},\quad \omega=2\pi f=ck$$

The core intuition here is that a changing $\vec E$ makes $\vec B$, and a changing $\vec B$ makes $\vec E$. The pair sustains itself and moves at a fixed speed.

*Example:* A wave has wavelength $400$ nm and $E_0=150$ V/m.
$$f=\frac{3.00\times10^{8}}{400\times10^{-9}}=7.5\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$$
$$B_0=\frac{E_0}{c}=\frac{150}{3.00\times10^{8}}=5.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm T$$

*Trap:* Placing $\vec E$ and $\vec B$ along the same line, or putting them out of phase. In vacuum they rise and fall together.

*Check:* In SI units $B_0$ is tiny compared with $E_0$.

name: Energy and momentum of fields
teach:
When you need energy flow, intensity, radiation pressure or field energy density, start from the Poynting vector $\vec S$, whose time average is the intensity $I$. Absorbing all the light gives pressure $I/c$, and perfect reflection reverses the momentum and gives twice as much. In a wave the electric and magnetic energy densities are equal. A point source of power $P_{\mathrm{src}}$ spreads its light over a sphere.
$$\vec S=\frac{\vec E\times\vec B}{\mu_0},\qquad I=\tfrac12\varepsilon_0cE_0^{2},\qquad P_{\mathrm{abs}}=\frac Ic,\qquad P_{\mathrm{refl}}=\frac{2I}{c},\qquad I=\frac{P_{\mathrm{src}}}{4\pi r^{2}}$$
$$u=\tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^{2}+\frac{B^{2}}{2\mu_0},\qquad u_{\mathrm{avg}}=\tfrac12\varepsilon_0E_0^{2}$$

The core intuition here is that fields carry energy and momentum. The energy flows along $\vec E\times\vec B$, and light pushes on what it hits.

*Example:* A beam has intensity $3.0\times10^{3}$ W/m$^2$ and falls on a perfect absorber.
$$E_0=\sqrt{\frac{2I}{\varepsilon_0c}}=\sqrt{\frac{6.0\times10^{3}}{(8.85\times10^{-12})(3.0\times10^{8})}}=1.5\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{V/m}$$
$$P=\frac Ic=\frac{3.0\times10^{3}}{3.0\times10^{8}}=1.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$$

*Trap:* Using $I/c$ for a mirror, which gets $2I/c$, or dropping the factor $\tfrac12$ that converts the peak field to an average.

*Check:* Radiation pressure is tiny in everyday conditions. A mirror in the same beam would feel exactly double.

name: Waves at interfaces and in media
teach:
When light crosses an interface or travels through a transparent medium of index $n$, the frequency stays fixed while the speed and wavelength change. Use Snell's law for the bend, $\lambda_0/n$ for the wavelength, and the reflectance $R$ at normal incidence. The transmitted fraction is $1-R$. At Brewster's angle $\theta_B$, measured from the normal, the reflected light has only one polarization.
$$n_1\sin\theta_1=n_2\sin\theta_2,\qquad v=\frac cn=\frac1{\sqrt{\varepsilon\mu}},\qquad \lambda=\frac{\lambda_0}{n},\qquad R=\left(\frac{n_1-n_2}{n_1+n_2}\right)^{2},\qquad \tan\theta_B=\frac{n_2}{n_1}$$

The core intuition here is that the source fixes the frequency. The medium changes the speed, so the wavelength changes in proportion.

*Example:* Red light of $630$ nm in air meets a plastic of $n=1.40$ at normal incidence.
$$\lambda=\frac{630}{1.40}=450\ \mathrm{nm},\qquad R=\left(\frac{1.0-1.4}{1.0+1.4}\right)^{2}=0.028$$

*Trap:* Thinking the frequency changes inside the medium. The speed and wavelength change, but the oscillation rate does not.

*Check:* A few percent reflects from an ordinary transparent surface, and the wavelength shrinks inside the denser medium.

name: Radiation from charges
teach:
If a charge accelerates, or an oscillating charge acts as a source of waves, take the power from the Larmor formula with $c=3.0\times10^{8}$ m/s. It depends on the acceleration squared and not on the mass. A charge oscillating with amplitude $x_0$ at angular frequency $\omega$ has acceleration amplitude $\omega^{2}x_0$, so its power grows as $\omega^{4}$. A dipole radiates most perpendicular to its axis and nothing along it.
$$P=\frac{q^{2}a^{2}}{6\pi\varepsilon_0c^{3}},\qquad a_{\max}=\omega^{2}x_0\ \Rightarrow\ P\propto\omega^{4},\qquad I\propto\sin^{2}\theta\ \text{(dipole)}$$

The core intuition here is that only a changing field can detach from its source and travel away. A charge at constant velocity has a steady field and radiates nothing.

*Example:* An electron accelerates at $1.0\times10^{20}$ m/s$^2$.
$$P=\frac{(1.6\times10^{-19})^{2}(1.0\times10^{20})^{2}}{6\pi(8.85\times10^{-12})(3.0\times10^{8})^{3}}=5.7\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm W$$

*Trap:* Expecting steady motion to radiate, or treating power as linear in acceleration.

*Check:* Doubling the acceleration multiplies the power by four.

name: Generalized coordinates
teach:
When a system has constraints, such as a rigid rod between two particles or a bead on a wire, pick variables that already respect them. For $N$ particles with $k$ independent constraints, the number of independent coordinates is $n=3N-k$. Choose $n$ variables, such as angles or lengths, that fix the whole configuration. Write each position in them, differentiate, and form $T$ and $V$ from those variables alone. If the constraint itself moves, that motion still contributes to $T$.
$$n = 3N - k,\qquad T=\sum_i\tfrac12 m_i\,|\dot{\vec r}_i|^{2}$$

The core intuition here is that a constraint removes freedom. Coordinates that ignore it are not independent, so equations written in them carry unknown constraint forces.

*Example:* Two masses are joined by a rigid rod and move freely in three dimensions.
$$n = 3(2) - 1 = 5$$
Use three coordinates for the centre of mass and two angles for the rod direction. For a pendulum bob at $x=\ell\sin\theta$, $y=-\ell\cos\theta$:
$$\dot x^{2}+\dot y^{2}=\ell^{2}\dot\theta^{2}\ \Rightarrow\ T=\tfrac12m\ell^{2}\dot\theta^{2}$$

*Trap:* Keeping all Cartesian coordinates and forgetting the constraints, or counting a velocity as a coordinate.

*Check:* A single free rigid body in space should give six variables.

name: Lagrange equations
teach:
